Franz Joseph Haydn, born of staunch Catholic parents at Rohrau in Austria on 1 April 1732 and died at Gumpendorf, Vienna, on 31 May 1809. He was a composer whose industry, more than any teacher, made him a master. He began in the choir school of St. Stephen's, Vienna, singing there nine years and yielding his solo place to his younger brother Michael when his voice changed. He seized every chance to learn music, under the influence of Emanuel Bach, Dittersdorf, and Porpora, though his achievements owe more to incessant work than to instruction.

By 1756 he ranked among Vienna's first music masters, and in 1759 he became vice-capellmeister to Count Morzin, whose country orchestra required daily divertimenti, a splendid school of instrumentation.

Johann Michael Haydn, younger brother of Joseph Haydn, made his career in church music at Salzburg. Born at Rohrau in Austria in 1737, he sang as a boy in the choir of St. Stephen's Cathedral in Vienna, where his older brother helped train him. From 1762 he served as orchestra conductor and organist under the prince-archbishop of Salzburg, posts he held for nearly forty-four years until his death in 1806.

Early on, employers and fellow musicians, including Leopold and Wolfgang Mozart, found his work and conduct wanting. His wife, the court singer Maria Magdalena Lipp, is credited with turning him toward steady industry. The entry then surveys a vast sacred output: twenty-four masses, two requiems, over a hundred graduals, dozens of offertories, plus litanies, vespers, cantatas, oratorios, operas, and instrumental works.
haydn:
J. Cuthbert Hadden, a Scottish music writer, told the life of Joseph Haydn for the Master Musicians series, in the fullest English account of its day. Hadden built on Dr. Pohl's German biography, finished after Pohl's death by Mandyczewski. Edinburgh saw the book issued in September 1902. Haydn's calm career, Hadden argues, makes a happy change from tragic composer tales.

Chapters trace a wheelwright's son from Rohrau to a choir desk at St Stephen's in Vienna. Dismissed when his voice broke, Haydn scraped lessons and attic composing into the Eisenstadt post. Nearly thirty years serving the Esterhazy princes at Esterhaz fill the chapters. Two London visits in the 1790s brought fame, money, and the symphonies written there. The Creation and The Seasons crown the late years before a Vienna old age. Appendices print Haydn's will, a catalogue of works, a bibliography, notes on his brothers, and letters for students.
